name: Silver peso (piece of eight)
what: The Spanish real de a ocho, a coin of about 27 g of silver struck from American silver from the 1530s. It was the first world currency, and the US dollar, Chinese yuan and Japanese yen all descend from it.
why: Most of it ended up in China. Following one coin shows the Potosí mines, the Spanish treasure fleets, the Manila galleons and Ming China's hunger for silver tied into the first global economy.
now: Legal tender in the United States until 1857; its descendants are the dollar, the peso, the yuan and the yen.

sources.cite: Flynn, D. O. & Giráldez, A. (1995). Born with a 'Silver Spoon': The Origin of World Trade in 1571. Journal of World History 6(2).
Lane, K. (2019). Potosí: The Silver City That Changed the World. University of California Press.
von Glahn, R. (1996). Fountain of Fortune: Money and Monetary Policy in China, 1000-1700. University of California Press.

stops.note: The first mint in the Americas opened in Mexico City in 1535-1536, coining silver from Taxco and, after 1546, from the great Zacatecas mines.

stops.owner: Spanish Crown, mine owners, mita labourers
stops.note: Silver was found in the Cerro Rico in 1545. Using mercury and the forced labour of the mita, Potosí became one of the largest cities in the world; a mint opened in 1572 to strike rough "cob" coins on the spot.
stops.meet: a mita labourer, a mine owner or a merchant in Potosí

stops.note: Llama and mule trains carried bars and coins down from 4,000 m to the Pacific port of Arica.
From 1565, when Urdaneta found the way back east across the Pacific, Acapulco was the American end of the Manila galleon route.

Spain founded Manila in 1571. Flynn and Giráldez date the birth of world trade to this year: every continent was now linked by regular trade, with silver going west and silk and porcelain coming east.
After the Ming reopened private sea trade at Yuegang in 1567, junks carried American silver home from Manila by the ton. China held perhaps a quarter of humanity and wanted silver for taxes.
Zhang Juzheng's Single Whip reform, extended across the empire around 1581, had taxes and labour duties paid in silver. Much of the silver that paid them had been mined in Potosí and Japan.
Peruvian silver went by sea to Panama, across the isthmus by mule, and waited at Nombre de Dios (Portobelo after 1597) for the galleons of the Tierra Firme fleet.
The fleets met at Havana and sailed home together in convoy. Everything was registered at Seville's Casa de Contratación, and the Crown took its fifth, the quinto real.
Spain's kings borrowed against the next fleet. Much of the silver went straight to their Genoese bankers, in what historians call the century of the Genoese (1557-1627).

stops.place: Antwerp and the Army of Flanders
stops.note: Coins paid the soldiers who marched the Spanish Road from Italy to the Netherlands. Unpaid wages caused mutinies, including the sack of Antwerp in 1576.
European companies had little India wanted except silver, so American coins paid for Indian cotton cloth at Surat and were reminted as Mughal rupees.
Spanish dollars were the money of the Canton trade. Chinese merchants struck small "chop" marks into each coin they tested, so many surviving pesos are covered in them.
The Coinage Act of 1792 defined the new US dollar by the Spanish dollar's silver content. Spanish and Mexican dollars stayed legal tender in the US until 1857.
Meiji Japan's new yen of 1871 was made the same weight of silver as the Mexican peso dollar that circulated in East Asian ports.
The Guangdong mint struck China's first machine-made silver dollars on the peso's weight in 1889. The Chinese word for these round coins, yuan, became the name of the currency.
